title: The LORD's Anointed
sum: The LORD speaks to Cyrus, the Persian king, and calls him "his anointed", the only foreigner in the Bible to bear the title. God will go ahead of him, smash Babylon's bronze gates and hand over its hidden treasures, not for Cyrus's sake but for Israel's, and so that the whole world will know that there is no God but the LORD. The oracle climbs to its boldest line: "I make peace and create disaster" (45:7). Nothing, light or dark, lies outside his rule.

Those who object to a pagan deliverer are answered with the potter and the clay (45:9–13). Then the nations come to Zion in chains of their own choosing and confess, "Surely God is among you" (45:14). The chapter ends with an invitation to the whole earth, "Turn to me and be saved", and an oath that every knee will bend and every tongue swear, words Paul later applies to the judgment of God and to Jesus (Romans 14:11; Philippians 2:10–11).
readings: Read as prophecy named ahead

On the traditional view the LORD names Cyrus some 150 years before his birth, and the chapter's argument depends on it: the God who announces events before they happen is the only God (45:21). Josephus says Cyrus read this oracle and was moved to free the Jews (Antiquities 11.5–6).
Read as words to exiles watching Cyrus

On the critical view a prophet in Babylon sees Cyrus's victories and announces that Israel's God, not Marduk, is behind them. The Cyrus Cylinder, in which Marduk chooses Cyrus and calls him by name, shows how bold the claim was: the prophet takes the language of Babylon's own propaganda and gives it to the LORD.
Read as the gospel of the nations

For Christian readers the chapter's horizon is the whole world. The God who uses Cyrus invites all the ends of the earth to turn to him, and the oath of 45:23 is fulfilled when every knee bows at the name of Jesus (Philippians 2:10–11).

views.H: Cyrus took Babylon in October 539 BC almost without a fight (Nabonidus Chronicle) and in 538 allowed exiles to return and rebuild the Temple (Ezra 1:1–4; 6:3–5). Historians read this chapter beside the Cyrus Cylinder, which uses strikingly similar language of the god taking Cyrus's hand and calling him by name.
views.C: Most critical scholars date 40–55 to about 545–539 BC and see 45:1–7 as the high point of the Cyrus oracles (41:1–5, 25; 44:24–28; 45:1–13; 46:11; 48:14–15). Some find in 45:7 an answer to Persian dualism, though the date and spread of Zoroastrian belief are debated; others read it simply as the strongest statement of one God's rule.
views.J: Jewish tradition reads Cyrus as an instrument raised up for Israel's sake. The Talmud (Megillah 12a) asks whether Cyrus was really the Messiah and answers that God spoke to the Messiah about Cyrus. The morning prayer Yotser Or quotes 45:7 with 'all things' for 'evil' (Berakhot 11b), and the Aleinu prayer ends each service with the words of 45:23.
views.X: The church fathers often read 45:1 christologically, and the Epistle of Barnabas quotes it with 'to Christ my Lord'. Paul uses 45:23 in Romans 14:11 for the final judgment and in Philippians 2:10–11 to give Jesus the worship the LORD here claims for himself. The Vulgate's 'let the earth bud forth a savior' (45:8) made the verse the Advent chant Rorate caeli.
views.F: Readers who look ahead note that 45:14–25 has not yet been fulfilled in full: the nations have not all come to Zion confessing that God is among her, nor has every tongue sworn by the LORD. They read the chapter's end as the last day, when all creation acknowledges the one God (Philippians 2:10–11; Revelation 15:4).

deep.b:
For Isaiah 45–55 the Plain is translated from the Leningrad Codex (AD 1008), verse by verse from a word-for-word rendering. The Dead Sea Scrolls were read for every verse in the transcriptions of Martin Abegg, James Bowley and Edward Cook (ETCBC dss): the Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a, about 125 BC, complete for these chapters), 1QIsa-b (1Q8), and the Cave 4 copies 4QIsa-b (4Q56), 4QIsa-c (4Q57), 4QIsa-d (4Q58) and 4QIsa-q (4Q69a) where they survive. The Talmud passages cited (Berakhot 5a, 11b and 64a; Sanhedrin 98b; Sotah 14a) were read in the Sefaria edition, and the Epistle of Barnabas in Lightfoot's translation. The Targum of Isaiah is cited as reported by Bruce Chilton's translation, and Ziegler's Göttingen Greek, the Latin Vulgate, the Syriac and the medieval Jewish commentators as reported by the editions and commentaries named in each note.

deep.h: Cyrus by name: the authorship question at its sharpest
deep.b:
Isaiah 44:28–45:1 names Cyrus, who began to rule about 559 BC, while Isaiah son of Amoz prophesied about 740–700 BC. The two views, given at full strength in the book's opening pages and at 44:28, meet here.

The traditional view, held by Jewish and Christian interpreters until modern times and by many today (Young, Oswalt, Motyer), sees the naming as the point of the passage. The chapters argue again and again that the LORD alone foretells events (41:21–29; 44:7; 45:21; 46:10; 48:3–5); a prophecy of Cyrus given after his rise would undercut that argument. The New Testament quotes these chapters as 'Isaiah' (Matthew 3:3; 12:17; John 12:38–41), and Josephus reports that Cyrus read the prophecy.

The critical view, the consensus since Döderlein (1775) and Duhm (1892), notes that 40–55 never mentions Hezekiah or Assyria as present, speaks to exiles already in Babylon (47:6; 48:20), and treats Cyrus as a figure already on the move (41:2–3, 25). Prophets elsewhere speak to their own generation, and the 'first things' now fulfilled (48:3) may be earlier prophecies. On this view the prophet's claim is that Cyrus's career fulfills the LORD's long purpose.

Both views agree on the passage's message: Israel's God directs the rise and fall of empires for the sake of his people and the knowledge of his name among the nations.

Isaiah 45:7 is the most sweeping statement in the Bible of God's rule over both good and ill. The pair 'light and darkness', 'peace and ra'', is a merism: two opposites that together mean 'everything'. In context it explains the Cyrus oracle: the LORD sends the conqueror and the collapse of Babylon, rescue for some and ruin for others. Amos 3:6 and Lamentations 3:38 say the same.

The verse does not set out a theory of moral evil, and readers have handled it differently. The rabbis changed it in the daily blessing to 'who makes peace and creates all things' (Berakhot 11b), honoring the verse while avoiding saying aloud that God creates evil. Aquinas cited it for the distinction between the evil of punishment, which God causes, and the evil of fault, which he does not (Summa I, q. 49, a. 2). Calvin said the 'evil' here is adversity, not sin. Others see a polemic against a Persian belief in two rival gods of light and darkness. The card on this page shows how the churches answer the wider question.

traditions.q: "I make peace and create disaster" (45:7). In what sense does God create evil?
views: God ordains whatever comes to pass, including calamity and judgment, yet he is not the author of sin (Westminster Confession 3.1; 5.4). Calvin reads 'evil' here as the adversity God sends, not sin, and attacks those who make God the author of wickedness.

Luther held that God works all in all, even in the wicked, but the evil comes from the corrupt will he works through, like a rider on a lame horse; the hidden will of God is not to be searched out (The Bondage of the Will).

God is in no way the cause of moral evil but permits it, and can draw good from it (Catechism 311–312). Aquinas cites this verse: God is the cause of the evil of punishment, which serves justice, but not of the evil of fault (Summa I, q. 49, a. 2).

Scripture often calls afflictions 'evil' and speaks of what God permits as if he did it; God wills only good, and evil comes from the free choice of creatures (John of Damascus, Exact Exposition 4.19).

Wesley taught that God permits sin but never decrees it, and he rejected any teaching that makes God the cause of sin (sermon Free Grace, 1739). The verse speaks of God's control of events and of judgment, not of his willing sin.

title: Gods Who Are Carried
sum: Babylon's great gods, Bel and Nebo, are pictured loaded on weary animals and dragged into captivity, too heavy to save anyone, unable even to save themselves. Against them stands the LORD, who has carried Israel since birth and will carry them into old age: "I made you, and I will bear you." Idols are made to order from gold and silver, set on a stand and cannot move or answer.

The second half returns to the argument from prophecy. The LORD announces the end from the beginning; his plan stands. He calls 'a bird of prey from the east', Cyrus, and brings his righteousness and salvation near to stubborn hearers who think rescue is far away.
readings: Read as satire

The chapter is a cartoon in words: the gods that were paraded through Babylon at the New Year festival are now freight on a donkey's back. The joke is theological: a god you must carry cannot carry you.
Read as pastoral comfort
The heart of the chapter is 46:3–4: the God who has carried his people from the womb will carry them to gray hair. For exiles grown old in Babylon the promise is personal.

views.H: Bel (Marduk) and Nebo (Nabu) were the chief gods of Babylon and Borsippa. Before Cyrus took Babylon, Nabonidus brought the gods of other cities into the capital; Cyrus says he returned them (Cyrus Cylinder). Babylon's own gods were not carried off in 539, which suggests the scene is taunt rather than report.
views.C: Critical scholars read 46 as a disputation addressed to exiles tempted to credit Babylon's gods, written before the fall of the city; that Cyrus did not in fact deport Marduk is often taken as evidence that the oracle came before the event.
views.J: Rashi reads Bel and Nebo as Babylon's idols humiliated at its fall. In the Ashkenazi prayer book 46:4, 'Till you grow old, I am he', is recited at the end of every service after the Aleinu prayer, with Proverbs 3:25 and Isaiah 8:10.
views.X: Christian preachers have long used 46:4 as a promise to the aged. John's Gospel echoes the 'I am he' of these chapters in Jesus's absolute 'I am' (John 8:24, 28, 58).
views.F: Futurist readers see the fall of Babylon's gods as a pattern of the final overthrow of idolatry when 'the idols will utterly vanish' (2:18) and Babylon falls for good (Revelation 18).

title: The Fall of Lady Babylon
sum: A taunt song over Babylon, the empire that destroyed Jerusalem in 587 BC, pictured as a pampered queen who has never known hardship. She must come down from her throne to sit in the dust, grind grain like a slave girl and wade the rivers into exile. God gave his people into her hand in anger, but she showed them no pity and thought her reign would last forever.

She boasts in God's own words, "I am, and besides me there is nothing", and is sure she will never be widowed or bereaved. Both disasters will come in one day. Her famous magic and her star-watchers, who mapped the sky and announced each month's fortunes, cannot charm the ruin away. Her trading partners will scatter, and no one will save her.
readings: Read as history

The chapter reflects real features of Babylon: its long imperial pride, its practice of deportation, its vast tradition of omens and astronomy. Babylon did fall, though to Cyrus in a bloodless takeover, not in the burning of 47:14.
Read as type

Revelation 17–18 takes up this chapter for 'Babylon the great', the world power of its own day: the queen who says she is no widow (Revelation 18:7), the plagues in one day, the merchants mourning. For many readers 'Babylon' becomes the name for every proud empire.

views.H: Babylon fell to Cyrus in October 539 BC; Xerxes later put down Babylonian revolts (484 BC). The city declined under the Seleucids and was largely abandoned by the first centuries AD. Its astronomical diaries, kept from about 750 BC, are the longest scientific record of the ancient world.
views.C: Form critics see a taunt song, modeled on the funeral lament, like 14:4–21 over the king of Babylon. The chapter's 'Daughter Babylon' is the counterpart of 'Daughter Zion' in 49–54: the one goes down into the dust as the other rises from it.
views.J: Jewish interpreters read Babylon's fall as God's justice on a nation that went beyond its commission (47:6), a theme also of Zechariah 1:15. Rashi explains the star-watchers as Babylon's astrologers, the 'Chaldeans' of Daniel.
views.X: Revelation 18:7–8 quotes 47:7–9, and the call of 48:20 becomes Revelation 18:4. Christian readers have applied the chapter to Rome, to persecuting powers and to the self-sufficient city of every age.
views.F: Futurist readers hold that the Babylon of Revelation 17–18 is a power still to come, and that this chapter will have a final fulfillment in its sudden fall 'in one day' (Revelation 18:8).

title: Told Ahead of Time
sum: The last chapter of the Cyrus section is the sternest. Israel swears by the LORD's name, but not honestly. The LORD foretold events long before so that this stubborn people, iron-necked and bronze-browed, could not credit an idol. Now he announces new things never heard before. He has refined Israel in the furnace of misery and saves them for his own name's sake, not for their merit.

The first and the last calls Cyrus, whom he loves, against Babylon. A voice says, 'the Lord GOD has sent me, and his Spirit'. God laments what might have been if Israel had obeyed: peace like a river. Then the command rings out: "Go out from Babylon!" and the release is told in the words of the exodus. A refrain closes the section: the wicked have no peace.
readings: Read as indictment and grace

The chapter holds together blunt accusation and free grace: Israel is a rebel from the womb (48:8), yet God refuses to cut them off, for the sake of his name (48:9–11). The release from Babylon is undeserved.
Read as the end of a section
Many readers divide 40–66 into three blocks of nine chapters. Chapter 48 ends the first: Cyrus and Babylon are not mentioned again, and from 49 the servant and Zion take center stage.

views.H: Cyrus's decree (Ezra 1:1–4) allowed exiles to leave Babylon from 538 BC. The returns under Sheshbazzar and Zerubbabel (Ezra 1–2) were modest; many Jews stayed in Babylonia, where a major Jewish center flourished for centuries and produced the Babylonian Talmud.
views.C: Critics note that 48 mixes harsh accusation (48:1–11) with the joyful call of 48:20–21, and many think a later editor sharpened the chapter's criticism of Israel. The voice in 48:16b is often taken as the prophet's own claim to commission, like 61:1.
views.J: The Targum renders 48:16 'the LORD God has sent me, and his Memra'. Jewish readers note that most exiles did not answer the call of 48:20; in the Talmud (Yoma 9b) Resh Lakish says that if Israel had gone up together like a wall in Ezra's day, the Second Temple would not have lacked God's presence.
views.X: The church fathers often read 48:16 as a glimpse of the Trinity: the Lord GOD and his Spirit sending the speaker. Paul's 'water from the rock' (1 Corinthians 10:4) and Revelation's 'Come out of her, my people' (Revelation 18:4) both take up this chapter's last verses.
views.F: Futurist readers hear in 48:20 a final call to God's people to separate from the last 'Babylon' before its fall (Revelation 18:4).

title: A Light to the Nations
sum: The servant speaks for the first time in his own voice, to the far coasts. Called before birth, his mouth made a sharp sword, he hears God name him: "You are my servant, Israel." He feels he has worn himself out for nothing, but God gives him a larger task: not only to bring Jacob back, but to be a light to the nations, so that God's salvation reaches the ends of the earth. The despised slave of rulers will see kings rise before him.

Then Zion speaks: "The LORD has forgotten me." God answers with one of Scripture's tenderest images: a mother may forget her nursing child, "but as for me, I will never forget you"; her name is carved on his palms. Her children are coming home in such numbers that the ruined city will be too small. Kings will carry them, and the tyrant's captives will be taken back.
readings: Read with the servant as Israel

The servant is named Israel (49:3), and his task is Israel's calling: to restore the people's own life and be God's light among the nations (42:6; 60:3). This is the main Jewish reading, and many modern scholars hold a version of it.
Read with the servant as one person

The servant has a mission to Israel (49:5–6), so he cannot simply be the nation. He may be the prophet, given Israel's name and task; Christians read him as Jesus, the one in whom Israel's vocation is fulfilled, whose light reaches the nations through the apostles (Acts 13:47).

views.H: The promise that 'kings will be your guardians' (49:23) was read in the Persian decrees that funded the Temple and protected the returnees (Ezra 6:8–10; 7:21–26). The Syene of 49:12 (Aswan) had a Jewish colony at Elephantine whose papyri, from the 400s BC, survive.
views.C: Duhm (1892) first set apart the four 'servant songs' (42:1–4; 49:1–6; 50:4–9; 52:13–53:12) as a separate source. Many now doubt the songs ever stood apart (Mettinger) and read 49:1–6 as part of its context, in which the servant is Israel or the prophet who takes up Israel's task after Israel's failure (49:4).
views.J: Rashi, Ibn Ezra and Kimchi read the servant here as Israel (or as the prophet speaking for Israel), following the explicit 'Israel' of 49:3. 49:14–51:3 is the haftarah of consolation for Ekev, and Zion's complaint and God's answer (49:14–16) are favorite texts of Jewish comfort.
views.X: Simeon calls the infant Jesus 'a light for revelation to the nations' (Luke 2:32), and Paul and Barnabas quote 49:6 as their commission (Acts 13:47). Paul applies 49:8 to the present 'day of salvation' (2 Corinthians 6:2) and describes his own call in the words of 49:1 (Galatians 1:15). The liturgy reads 49:1–6 on the Tuesday of Holy Week.
views.F: Futurist readers see the regathering of 49:8–26, with kings and queens carrying Israel's children home, as a promise for Israel at the end, still unfulfilled in full; some point to the return of Jews to the land in modern times as its beginning.

deep.h: "You are my servant, Israel": who is the servant?
deep.b:
Isaiah 49:3 puts the identity question in its sharpest form. In 41:8–9, 44:1–2 and 44:21 'my servant' is plainly Jacob-Israel, the people. In 42:18–20 the servant is blind and deaf. Yet the servant of 49:1–6 has a mission to Israel, to bring Jacob back (49:5), and in 50:4–9 and 52:13–53:12 he suffers innocently for others.

The servant as Israel. The text names him Israel, and every ancient witness has the name (see the variant). Jewish interpreters from the Middle Ages (Rashi, Ibn Ezra, Kimchi) read the songs as Israel's vocation and suffering among the nations. Some modern scholars refine this: the faithful within Israel, an ideal Israel, or the exiles in Babylon who are to restore the rest.

The servant as an individual. Others note the personal language (womb, mother, mouth) and the mission to Israel. Candidates include the prophet himself (49:4 sounds like a prophet's complaint), Jeremiah, Moses and Zerubbabel. Christians, following the New Testament, read the servant as Jesus, who takes on Israel's name and calling as Israel's representative.

Between the two. H. Wheeler Robinson's idea of 'corporate personality' and similar views see the servant moving between the people and one who embodies it. Brevard Childs reads the canonical book so that the servant called Israel in 49:3 is the one who carries out Israel's task when Israel itself has failed. Christopher North's survey (1948, 1956) remains the fullest history of the debate.

title: The Servant Who Listens
sum: The LORD asks for the certificate of divorce he gave mother Zion, or the creditor he sold her children to: there are none. Israel was sent away for its sins, but the marriage was never ended, and God owes no one. His hand is not too short to save: he dries up the sea and dresses the sky in black. Yet when he called, no one answered.

Then the servant speaks again, in the third song (50:4–9). God gave him a disciple's tongue to sustain the weary, and opened his ear each morning. He did not turn back. He gave his back to the floggers and his cheeks to those who pulled his beard, and did not hide his face from spitting. Because the Lord GOD helps him, he sets his face like flint, sure that his judge will declare him in the right. The chapter ends with a choice between trusting God in the dark and walking by one's own fire.
readings: Read as the prophet's own suffering
Rashi and Ibn Ezra take the speaker to be the prophet, mocked and beaten for his message, yet confident in God. The song never uses the word 'servant'; only 50:10 makes the link.
Read as the Passion

views.H: Debt slavery, in which children could be sold to pay a father's debts (2 Kings 4:1; Nehemiah 5:5), and divorce by written certificate (Deuteronomy 24:1–4) were real practices; 50:1 uses both to say that God's covenant with Israel was never dissolved.
views.C: Critics identify 50:4–9 as the third servant song, often with 50:10–11 as a later comment. Many read it as a prophet's personal lament of confidence, in the style of Jeremiah's 'confessions' (Jeremiah 11:18–20:18), and take the speaker as the prophet of 40–55 himself.
views.J: Jewish commentators read the speaker as the prophet, who endures abuse for the word he brings, or as Israel suffering among the nations. In the synagogue the song is read as part of the Ekev haftarah of consolation (49:14–51:3).
views.X: The Gospels' accounts of the mocking and flogging of Jesus echo 50:6, and Luke's 'he set his face to go to Jerusalem' (Luke 9:51) may echo 50:7. Paul's 'Who will bring a charge? It is God who justifies' (Romans 8:33–34) follows 50:8–9.
views.F: Futurist readers emphasize the vindication of 50:8–9, when the servant's accusers 'wear out like a garment', as a picture of the final judgment.

title: Wake Up, Arm of the LORD
sum: Three times the LORD calls 'Listen to me' to those who seek righteousness. Look back to Abraham and Sarah: one man, called and blessed, became many; so ruined Zion will become like Eden. God's teaching and justice will go out as light to the peoples, and his salvation will outlast heaven and earth, which will wear out like old clothes.

Then the people call on God: "Wake up, wake up, arm of the LORD!" They remember how he cut Rahab the sea dragon to pieces and dried the sea for the redeemed to cross. God answers, 'It is I who comfort you', and turns to Jerusalem, lying drunk in the streets from the cup of his fury. He takes the cup from her hand and gives it to her tormentors.
readings: Read as a call to remember
The chapter moves through Israel's memory: Abraham and Sarah (51:2), Eden (51:3), the victory at the sea (51:9–10). Each memory becomes a ground for hope in the present.
Read as myth reused

The 'Rahab' and 'dragon' of 51:9 belong to the ancient picture of God defeating the chaos waters. Isaiah applies it to the exodus and the return, so that the exiles in Babylon, the city of Marduk who slew the sea goddess, hear that their God is the true victor.

views.H: The return from exile involved crossing the Syrian desert, not the sea; the prophet pictures it as a new crossing to make the exiles see it as a second exodus.
views.C: Critics see in 51:9–52:2 a sequence of three 'wake up' calls (51:9, 17; 52:1), probably arranged deliberately. 51:11 repeats 35:10, one of several links that suggest chapters 34–35 were written or placed to bridge the book's two halves.

views.X: Christian readers hear in 51:6 the words of Jesus, 'Heaven and earth will be gone, but my words will never be gone' (Matthew 24:35), and in the cup of 51:17–22 the cup Jesus prays may pass from him (Matthew 26:39), which he drinks for others.
views.F: Futurist readers link 51:6 with the passing of heaven and earth before the new creation (2 Peter 3:10–13; Revelation 21:1), and the cup given to the oppressors with the bowls of wrath in Revelation 16.

title: Your God Is King
sum: "Wake up, wake up, Zion!" The cry that called on the LORD's arm in 51:9 now turns to the city itself. The captive city is told to shake off the dust, put on her festal clothes and loosen the chains from her neck. She was sold for nothing and will be bought back without money; Egypt, Assyria and now Babylon had no right to her, and God's name has been mocked long enough.

A runner appears on the mountains with good news: "Your God is King!" The lookouts shout as they see the LORD return to Zion, the ruins burst into song, and the whole earth sees his saving arm. The exiles are to leave Babylon clean, carrying the Temple vessels, not in a rush as from Egypt, with the LORD before and behind them. Then, at 52:13, the fourth servant song begins: the servant who will be high and lifted up, whose disfigurement once appalled many, will startle nations and silence kings.
readings: Read as the return to Zion
The chapter's first twelve verses are a drama of homecoming: the city wakes, the messenger arrives, the king returns, the exiles set out. The 'good news' of 52:7 is the end of exile.
Read as the gospel

The New Testament borrows the chapter's words for its own message: Paul quotes 52:7 for the preachers of the gospel (Romans 10:15), 52:5 for the dishonor of God's name (Romans 2:24), 52:11 for holiness (2 Corinthians 6:17), and 52:15 for his mission to the Gentiles (Romans 15:21). Jesus's announcement of the kingdom of God (Mark 1:14–15) echoes 52:7.

views.H: The vessels of 52:11 are those Nebuchadnezzar took from the Temple (2 Kings 25:13–15) and Cyrus returned to Sheshbazzar, 5,400 items by Ezra's count (Ezra 1:7–11).
views.C: Critics see 52:1–12 as the climax of the Zion poems that began at 40:9, with the messenger of 40:9 now arriving. Most hold that 52:13–53:12 was composed separately and placed here, though recent scholars stress how closely it is tied to its context (52:10 and 53:1, 'the LORD's arm').
views.J: 51:12–52:12 is the fourth haftarah of consolation, for Shoftim; the reading stops at 52:12, and the next haftarah begins at 54:1, so 52:13–53:12 is not read in the cycle. The Targum renders 52:7 'the kingdom of your God is revealed' and 52:13 'my servant the Messiah'.
views.X: Romans 10:15 quotes 52:7, Romans 15:21 quotes 52:15, and John 12:38 and Romans 10:16 quote 53:1, which continues the song. 11QMelchizedek, a Qumran text, applies 52:7 to the end time and calls the messenger 'the anointed of the Spirit'.
views.F: Futurist readers see 52:7–10, when 'every far end of the earth' sees God's salvation and the LORD returns to Zion, as a picture of the second coming and the kingdom on earth.

settings.readers: For later readers the song became the most debated passage in the book. The synagogue tradition read it of Israel suffering among the nations, or of the Messiah; the first Christians read it as the explanation of Jesus's death (Acts 8:32–35; 1 Peter 2:21–25). The churches read it on Good Friday.
views: Isaiah, about 700 BC, foresees a servant whose suffering lies far in the future; most Christian holders of this view take him to be the Messiah, Jesus, and the passage to be prophecy in the full sense.

A prophet among the exiles, about 540 BC, or a disciple after his death, wrote the song. Some think it reflects the actual suffering and death of a figure known to its first hearers (the prophet himself, on Whybray's and Mowinckel's early views); others think it portrays Israel in exile; many see a figure of the future.
The song is overheard as the nations' confession: Israel, the servant, hears that its oppressors will one day admit that Israel suffered for their sins (Rashi, Ibn Ezra, Kimchi).

title: The Servant Who Suffered for Many
sum: The song that began at 52:13 continues in a voice that says 'we'. Who could have believed it? The servant grew up like a scrawny shoot in dry ground, without looks or grandeur, despised and avoided, a man of pains who knew sickness well. 'We' thought God was punishing him. But it was our sicknesses he carried, our rebellions that pierced him; the discipline that made us whole fell on him, and through his welts we are healed. We had all strayed like sheep, and the LORD made our guilt fall on him.

He went silently, like a lamb to slaughter, through arrest and sentence, was cut off from the land of the living and given a grave with the wicked, though he had done no violence. Yet the LORD willed it: his life becomes a guilt offering, and he will see offspring and long days. In the closing verdict God speaks: out of his anguish he will see light; the righteous one, my servant, will make the many righteous. Because he poured out his life to death and was counted with the rebels, bearing the sin of many and pleading for them, he will share the spoil with the mighty.
readings: Read as Israel's song among the nations

The kings of 52:15 confess that the people they despised and crushed suffered for their sins, and they will see that people raised up. This is the main Jewish reading and is held by some Christian scholars as the song's first sense.
Read as a righteous sufferer of Israel's history
The song honors a prophet or leader whose innocent suffering and death benefited the community, as the Talmud reads it of Moses and Saadia of Jeremiah.
Read as the gospel of the cross

For the New Testament and the church the song describes Jesus: rejected, silent before his judges, crucified between criminals, buried with the rich, and raised to see his 'offspring'. 1 Peter 2:21–25 builds its whole teaching on suffering from it.

views.H: Readers who look for historical fulfillment point to Jesus's trial, scourging, silence before Pilate, death with criminals and burial in Joseph of Arimathea's tomb (Matthew 27:12–14, 38, 57–60). Others find the song's first fulfillment in the suffering of the exiles and the return under Cyrus.
views.C: Critical scholarship since Duhm (1892) has debated whether the servant is the prophet, Israel or an ideal figure, and whether he really dies (Whybray says no). Many now read the song in its book context as the climax of the servant theme, the figure through whom Israel's calling is fulfilled, without naming him. Debate also continues over whether the song teaches vicarious atonement; most say yes, with the guilt offering of 53:10 as the key (Janowski, Hermisson), while a minority (Orlinsky, Whybray) deny that it does.
views.J: Rashi, Ibn Ezra, Kimchi and Abravanel read the servant as Israel; the Targum and parts of the Talmud and Midrash read him as the Messiah, whose sufferings are either moved onto others (Targum) or accepted (Sanhedrin 98b). The passage is not read in the synagogue's yearly cycle of prophetic readings. Jewish writers since the Middle Ages have answered Christian readings point by point (Troki).
views.X: The church reads the chapter on Good Friday in the Catholic, Orthodox, Anglican and Lutheran traditions and in the Revised Common Lectionary. It shaped every theory of the atonement, from Anselm's satisfaction to the Reformers' penal substitution and modern 'Christus Victor' views, and gave Handel's Messiah 'He was despised', 'Surely he hath borne our griefs' and 'All we like sheep'.
views.F: Futurist readers often see 53:1–9 as the confession that Israel will make when it recognizes its Messiah at his return (Zechariah 12:10; Romans 11:26), reading the 'we' as Israel at the end of the age.

deep.b:
'About whom does the prophet say this, about himself or about someone else?' asks the Ethiopian official in Acts 8:34. The question has four main answers, each held by serious readers.

  1. Israel, the people, or its faithful core.
  2. An individual of Israel's past or present: the prophet, Moses, Jeremiah, Zerubbabel, King Jehoiachin, a martyr of the exile.
  3. The Messiah still to come, as in the Targum and some rabbinic texts.
  4. Jesus, as the New Testament and the church read it.

The answers are not all exclusive. Christian scholars often hold that the servant is Israel's calling fulfilled in one person; some Jewish readings hold that the Messiah embodies Israel's suffering. The sections below give each at its strongest.

deep.h: The servant as Israel: the Jewish reading at its strongest
deep.b:
This reading is old. Origen, about AD 248, reports Jewish teachers who said the prophecy referred 'to the whole people, regarded as one individual', scattered among the nations so that many might become proselytes (Against Celsus 1.55). Rashi, Ibn Ezra, Kimchi and Abravanel developed it, and it is the reading of most Jewish interpreters today.

The book names the servant. In 40–55 'my servant' is again and again Jacob-Israel (41:8–9; 44:1–2, 21; 45:4; 48:20), and 49:3 says outright 'You are my servant, Israel'. A reader of the book arriving at 52:13 has every reason to hear Israel.

The speakers are the nations. The song begins with 'many nations' and 'kings' who are astonished (52:15); the 'we' of 53:1 most naturally continues with them. Their confession, 'we thought of him as stricken, struck down by God', is the nations' verdict on exiled Israel, reversed when they see Israel exalted (compare 49:7, 23; 60:14).

Personification is normal. Isaiah pictures Zion as a mother and a bride (49:14–21; 54:1–8); Lamentations 3 speaks of Jerusalem's suffering in the voice of 'the man who has seen affliction'. A suffering 'man of pains' can be a people.

The grammar leans plural. Lamo, 'to them' (53:8), and bemotav, 'in his deaths' (53:9), suit a collective, as Jewish writers from the Middle Ages (Troki, Faith Strengthened) pointed out.

The rewards fit a nation. 'He will see offspring; he will lengthen his days' (53:10) are blessings of descendants and long life, which Israel receives as its tents are widened (54:1–3). Exile was national death and burial, and the return is resurrection (Ezekiel 37:11–14).

Vicarious suffering is real. On this reading the song does not say Israel was sinless, but that it suffered more than its share, and that the nations' well-being came through its pain; 53:9 says it did no violence to them. The song then becomes the nations' confession of what they did to Israel, a reading that weighed heavily after centuries of Christian persecution of Jews.

deep.h: An individual: the prophet, Moses, Jeremiah, Zerubbabel
deep.b:
Many readers, Jewish and Christian, have found the song too personal for a nation: a man with a face, a grave and a trial, who suffers for 'my people' (53:8) though innocent (53:9), while Israel elsewhere in 40–55 is guilty (42:24; 43:24; 48:8). Their candidates include:

  • Moses, who offered his life for Israel after the golden calf. Rabbi Simlai reads 53:12 of him (Babylonian Talmud, Sotah 14a), and Ernst Sellin proposed him in 1922.
  • Jeremiah, 'like a gentle lamb led to the slaughter' (Jeremiah 11:19), as Saadia Gaon (900s) read it, and Hugo Grotius (1644), who saw Jeremiah first and Christ in a further sense.
  • Zerubbabel or King Jehoiachin, leaders of the exiled royal line (Sellin's earlier proposals, 1898 and 1901).
  • The prophet himself, persecuted and perhaps killed, the song being written by his disciples (the early Mowinckel, 1921); or rescued from prison rather than killed, the song being a thanksgiving (Whybray, 1978). Duhm himself thought of an unknown teacher of the Law who died of a skin disease.

No candidate has won general agreement, and the variety shows that the song does not name its subject.

deep.h: The Messiah in the Targum and the rabbis
deep.b:
The Targum of Isaiah, the Aramaic paraphrase used in synagogues and compiled in the early centuries AD, names the servant 'my servant the Messiah' (52:13). But it reshapes the song around a triumphant Messiah. The disfigurement belongs to Israel in exile; the Messiah 'will build the sanctuary which was profaned for our sins' (53:5), will 'hand over the mighty nations like a lamb to the slaughter' (53:7), and will pray for the people's sins, which are forgiven for his sake. The suffering falls on the nations and on the wicked, not on him (Chilton).

Other rabbinic texts apply the song's suffering to the Messiah more directly. The Talmud calls him 'the leper of the house of Rabbi' from 53:4 (Sanhedrin 98b), and Ruth Rabbah 5:6 applies 53:5 to his sufferings. S. R. Driver and Adolf Neubauer gathered the Jewish commentaries on the chapter in 1876–1877 and showed that the messianic reading continued in some medieval writers alongside the reading as Israel. Maimonides' picture of the Messiah as a king who restores Israel (Mishneh Torah, Kings 11) has no dying Messiah, which shaped later Jewish answers to Christian readings.

The New Testament cites the song more than any other Old Testament passage of its length, and in every case of Jesus:

  • 53:1 in John 12:38 and Romans 10:16, for unbelief.
  • 53:4 in Matthew 8:17, for his healings.
  • 53:7–8 in Acts 8:32–35, where Philip, 'starting from this Scripture', tells the Ethiopian about Jesus.
  • 53:9, 5, 6 in 1 Peter 2:22–25, the longest use, for Christ's innocent suffering 'for you'.
  • 53:12 in Luke 22:37, in Jesus's own words before his arrest.
  • 52:15 in Romans 15:21, for Paul's mission.

Echoes are widely seen in Mark 10:45 ('to give his life as a ransom for many'), Mark 14:24, Romans 4:25 ('handed over for our trespasses'), Romans 5:19 and Philippians 2:6–11. How early the song shaped Jesus's own understanding of his death is debated: Morna Hooker (1959) argued that the links are few and late; Peter Stuhlmacher, Martin Hengel and others answer that Isaiah 53 stands behind the earliest creeds ('Christ died for our sins in line with the Scriptures', 1 Corinthians 15:3). Outside the New Testament, 1 Clement 16 (about AD 96) quotes the whole song, and Justin Martyr's Dialogue with Trypho argues it against a Jewish opponent.

Christian readers answer the Israel reading by pointing to 'my people' in 53:8 (Origen), to the servant's innocence, which Isaiah never claims for the nation (contrast 1:4; 43:24; 48:8), and to his willing silence (53:7). Many also note that Wisdom of Solomon 2–5, a Jewish book of the first century BC, already uses the song for a righteous man who is condemned and then vindicated before his persecutors.

Every Qumran copy that survives agrees with the Hebrew in most of the song, but several readings matter, and each has a variant entry: 'my people' or 'his people' (53:8); 'in his deaths' and 'rich men' (53:9); 'made him sick' or 'pierced him' (53:10); 'he will see light' (53:11), which the Plain follows with the Great Isaiah Scroll, 1QIsa-b, 4QIsa-d and the Greek; and 'sins of many' and 'for their rebellions' (53:12). The word yazzeh in 52:15 is the same in all the scrolls; the question there is what it means, 'startle' or 'sprinkle' (see the note).

The Greek is a free translation that often reads differently: 'he was led to death' for 'the blow fell on him' (53:8), 'I will give the wicked for his burial' (53:9), 'the Lord wishes to cleanse him from the blow' (53:10). Acts 8:32–33 and 1 Peter 2:22 quote this Greek form.

settings.by: A group speaking as 'we': the kings and nations of 52:15, or Israel, or the prophet and his followers (debated)
settings.to: Spoken before God and anyone who hears; the reader overhears a confession
settings.when: After seeing the servant exalted (52:13–15)
settings.why: To confess that 'we' misjudged the servant's suffering as God's punishment of him, when it was for 'our' rebellions, and that his wounds have brought 'our' healing
settings.readers: Jewish readers heard the nations' future confession about Israel; Christian readers made the words their own confession about Jesus (1 Peter 2:24–25).
views: The 'we' are the kings of 52:15, who confess what they did to the servant, Israel (Rashi, Ibn Ezra, Kimchi; many modern scholars).

The 'we' are Israel, or the faithful in Israel, confessing that they rejected the servant who suffered for them (most Christian interpreters; some modern scholars who read the servant as the prophet).

settings.to: The same hearers as 52:13
settings.when: Closing the song
settings.why: To declare that the servant's suffering achieves God's purpose: he will make the many righteous, and he receives the victor's share because he bore their sin
settings.readers: For later readers these lines became the basis for teaching that the servant's death was a substitution and that he intercedes for the guilty.
views: Traditional view: God's verdict on the Messiah, foretold by Isaiah about 700 BC.
Critical view: God's verdict on the servant, whether the prophet, Israel or a figure to come, announced to exiles about 540 BC.

traditions.q: The servant was 'crushed for our guilt', and 'the discipline that made us whole was on him' (53:5, 10). In what sense did Christ die in our place?
views: Christ bore the punishment due to sinners, and so satisfied God's justice in their place: this is penal substitution, read directly from 53:5–6 and 53:10 (Calvin, Institutes 2.16.5–6; Heidelberg Catechism, Q. 37). John Stott's The Cross of Christ is a modern statement.

Christ took the sinner's place under the law and its curse, and his obedience and suffering are counted to the believer as righteousness (Formula of Concord, Solid Declaration 3). Lutherans also stress, with Gustaf Aulén, Christ's victory over sin, death and the devil.

Christ's death fulfills the servant's 'offering for sin' (53:10) and makes satisfaction for the sins of all, offered in love and obedience to the Father (Catechism 615–616). Following Anselm and Aquinas, Catholic teaching speaks of satisfaction and merit rather than God punishing the Son.

Christ freely takes on our suffering and death to destroy death and heal human nature from within; Orthodox writers use the language of sacrifice and ransom but generally reject the idea that the Father needed to punish the Son before he could forgive.

traditions.q: "Through his welts we have healing" (53:5). Does the servant's suffering promise bodily healing to believers now?
views: Yes: deliverance from sickness is provided for in the atonement and is the privilege of all believers (Assemblies of God, Statement of Fundamental Truths 12, citing 53:4–5 and Matthew 8:16–17). Word of Faith teachers, following E. W. Kenyon, go further and teach that healing may be claimed by faith.

Christ's passion is the source of all healing, of soul and body, and the Church continues his care in the sacrament of the Anointing of the Sick, which sometimes brings bodily healing when it serves salvation (Catechism 1505, 1520). The verse speaks first of healing from sin.

The verse speaks of healing from sin (as 1 Peter 2:24 applies it); Matthew 8:17 was fulfilled in Jesus's earthly ministry. The atonement secures the resurrection of the body, not healing on demand now, though God may heal in answer to prayer (B. B. Warfield, Counterfeit Miracles).
Divided: Holiness and charismatic evangelicals teach healing in the atonement; many others hold that physical healing is a benefit of Christ's work fully received only at the resurrection.

title: Sing, Barren One
sum: After the servant's song, Zion is told to sing. The barren, deserted wife will have more children than the married one; she must widen her tent and lengthen its ropes, for her descendants will spread right and left and fill the empty towns. Her husband is her Maker, the Holy One of Israel. He abandoned her 'for a little moment' in a flood of anger, but with loyal love that never ends he takes her back. As he swore after Noah's flood never to flood the earth again, so he swears never again to rage at her. Mountains may move, but his covenant of peace will not.

The storm-tossed city will be rebuilt of jewels: lapis foundations, ruby battlements, gates of sparkling stone. All her children will be taught by the LORD. No weapon forged against her will succeed: this is the inheritance of 'the servants of the LORD'.
readings: Read as Zion's restoration
The chapter answers the servant's suffering with the people's renewal: the servant 'will see offspring' (53:10), and Zion's tent overflows with children.
Read as the church and the new Jerusalem

Paul quotes 54:1 for the 'Jerusalem above', mother of believers from every nation (Galatians 4:26–27), and Revelation builds its jeweled city from 54:11–12 (Revelation 21:18–21). Jesus quotes 54:13 in John 6:45.

views.H: Jerusalem was rebuilt slowly: the Temple was finished in 515 BC (Ezra 6:15) and the walls under Nehemiah about 445 BC. The jeweled city of 54:11–12 went beyond anything the returnees built, a gap that later readers (Tobit 13; Revelation 21) carried forward into hope.
views.C: Critics note that 54 joins two images, the barren wife (54:1–10) and the jeweled city (54:11–17), and that 54:17 introduces the plural 'servants', a theme of 56–66. Many see 54 as the answer to Lamentations, whose 'not comforted' (Lamentations 1:2, 9) is echoed in 54:11.
views.J: 54:1–10 is the fifth haftarah of consolation (Ki Tetse), and 54:11–55:5 the third (Re'eh). The Talmud's 'read not your children but your builders' (Berakhot 64a) on 54:13 is recited in the daily prayers. A Qumran commentary (4Q164) reads the jewels of 54:11–12 as the priests and leaders of the community.
views.X: Galatians 4:27 and 2 Clement 2 apply 54:1 to the church of the nations. 54:5–14 is read at the Easter Vigil in the Catholic liturgy. William Carey's sermon on 54:2–3 (1792) helped start the modern missionary movement.
views.F: Futurist readers see the city of jewels as the new Jerusalem 'coming down out of heaven from God' (Revelation 21:2, 19), and the promise that Zion will never again be shaken as fulfilled only in the age to come.

settings.to: Zion, pictured as a barren and abandoned wife
settings.when: After the servant song, as the exiles' release begins
settings.why: To turn Zion's shame into joy by promising children, a husband's return and an oath as firm as the covenant with Noah
settings.readers: For the collected book's later readers, the Jews back in Judah under Persian rule and the synagogue and church after them, the oracle was proof that the LORD had named the deliverer and kept his word.
views: Traditional view: Isaiah of Jerusalem, about 700 BC in Hezekiah's reign, wrote these words for a generation that would live in exile and see Cyrus rise, so that when it happened they would know the LORD had foretold it (48:3–5).

Critical view: a prophet among the exiles in Babylon in the 540s BC, as Cyrus conquered Media and Lydia and threatened Babylon, spoke to captives who had lived some fifty years under Babylonian rule; his words were later joined to the book of Isaiah.

title: Come to the Water
sum: The book of comfort ends with an invitation. Like a street-seller, the LORD calls the thirsty and the penniless to come and buy water, wine and milk for nothing. Why spend money on what does not satisfy? Listen and live. God will make an everlasting covenant with the people, the sure loyal love once promised to David, and nations they do not know will run to them.

Seek the LORD while he can be found; let the wicked turn back to the God who forgives abundantly, for his thoughts and ways are higher than ours as the heavens are above the earth. As rain and snow water the earth and do not go back until it bears seed and bread, God's word will not come back to him empty. The exiles will go out in joy, the hills singing and the trees clapping, and thorns will give way to cypress and myrtle, a lasting sign of the LORD's name.
readings: Read as the close of 40–55
The chapters that opened with God's word that 'will stand forever' (40:8) end with the word that does what it was sent to do (55:11). The new exodus of 55:12 completes the road of 40:3.
Read as wisdom's invitation

The call to come and eat echoes Wisdom's banquet (Proverbs 9:1–6). For Jewish readers it is the invitation to Torah; for Christian readers, Jesus's 'If anyone is thirsty, he should come to me' (John 7:37) and the last invitation of the Bible (Revelation 22:17).

views.H: The 'covenant with David' (55:3) is offered at a time when no Davidic king reigned; Zerubbabel, of David's line, governed Judah briefly under Persia (Haggai 2:20–23), and then the line disappears from power.
views.C: Many critical scholars read 55:3–5 as a 'democratization' of the Davidic covenant: the promises to the king now pass to the whole people (von Rad, Westermann). Others argue that the chapter still expects a Davidic ruler. The chapter is widely seen as an epilogue matching the prologue in 40:1–11.
views.J: 55:1–5 ends the Re'eh haftarah, and 55:6–56:8 is read in the afternoon service of public fast days. The rabbis read the 'water' of 55:1 as the Torah (Babylonian Talmud, Ta'anit 7a): as water flows to the low places, Torah stays with the humble.
views.X: Paul quotes the Greek of 55:3, 'the holy and sure things of David', in his sermon at Pisidian Antioch for the resurrection of Jesus (Acts 13:34). 55:1–11 is read at the Easter Vigil in the Catholic liturgy and in many Protestant churches. 55:10–11 is a classic text for the power of preaching.
views.F: Futurist readers see 55:12–13, nature rejoicing and the curse of thorns reversed, as the renewal of creation at the end (Romans 8:19–21; Revelation 22:3).
